Case Study 01

Kiosk POS — a touch-first payment experience for walk-up branch visitors

The company's branches ran enrollment sales on a legacy, cashier-only screen and a parallel paper process for holds and partial payments. I designed and built its replacement: an unattended, touch-only kiosk that a student, a minor, or a tutor paying on someone else's behalf can use without staff walking them through it.

RoleUX design (Figma) + front-end implementation, solo
UsersStudents (adult & minor), tutors, in-branch cashiers
StackReact, Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, Redux Toolkit / RTK Query
StatusIn production, 165+ routes, Nov 2025 – present

The problem

A single flow had to serve very different buyers — an adult enrolling themselves, a minor who needs a guardian, a tutor enrolling multiple children — on a public, touch-only screen, with zero staff narration. The old UI didn't distinguish these paths, which is exactly where cashier errors and paper workarounds crept in.

The constraint that shaped everything

This isn't a phone in someone's hand — it's a shared terminal in a branch lobby. Every screen had to answer three questions instantly: where am I in this process, what happens if I stop, and did my payment actually go through. Anxiety and ambiguity at a payment terminal are the enemy.

Design decisions

Why the screen looks the way it does

A dedicated kiosk UI kit

Built a component set specific to this context: a step indicator, a progress bar, skeleton / empty / loading states, and large, high-contrast selection cards.

Why → a shared public terminal can't rely on staff narration; the interface has to self-explain at every step, for users with a wide range of comfort with technology.

A mascot + a success moment (confetti)

A friendly character appears through the flow, and a short confetti animation marks a completed purchase before the thank-you screen.

Why → a payment kiosk in a school lobby reads as cold and transactional by default; this is a deliberate attempt to make it feel closer to a positive, calm interaction.

Explicit terminal states for every branch

Cash, card, processing, success, cancelled, and thank-you all exist as distinct screens — plus 11+ cash-handling and payment-hold scenarios (change, partial holds, surplus).

Why → an ambiguous "in-between" state at a cash register is where operator mistakes and disputes happen. Every branch needed an unambiguous end state.

A documented, shared design system

Color tokens, button/input patterns, and selection-card states are written down, not just implemented — so a second, related kiosk product stayed visually consistent.

Why → without a shared design file, written tokens are what keeps two codebases from drifting apart visually.

Real-time feedback while cash is inserted

The cash screen polls the bill validator live: the amount collected and a progress bar update the instant a note is accepted, from 0% up to a confirmable 100% — plus a partial-payment ("Apartar") path with a slider and quick 25%/50%/max shortcuts for holds.

Why → without live confirmation, a person feeding cash into a machine has no way to know it's actually being counted; the wait itself is the risk, not just the total. Same channel, two audiences: the staff terminal below reads the identical live feed, tied to a specific terminal ID — one real-time event, two screens that need it for different reasons.

The staff side

Kiosco Express — the cashier's companion terminal

The student-facing kiosk above isn't the whole system — a second, staff-operated app ("Kiosco Express") runs at the counter for card payments and in-branch cash handling. It picks a sede (campus) and caja (register), then opens the same real-time cash-counting channel the kiosk itself uses, so a cashier sees money being counted live instead of guessing.

Live production screen — Kiosco Express, step 1: pick a sede (campus), card-payment path
Live production screen — same step, cash-payment path; the CTA and downstream flow change with the method
Live production screen — step 2: select an active caja (register), with a last-used timestamp and status badge
Live production screen — step 3: cash collection tied to one terminal ID, "realtime: conectado", with a live Total / Ingresado / Faltante breakdown and a no-refund warning
Iteration note: the flow was adjusted against real feedback from cashiers and branch staff during rollout — closer to a demo shaping next week's build than a spec shaping a backlog.
Case Study 02

Public Conversion Site — enroll and pay in one flow

The public-facing site is where most students first meet the company. I designed and built the multi-step enrollment wizard shown below — objective, modality, course, package, group, purchase, and personal data — so a visitor can go from "what do I need" to a completed, paid enrollment without leaving the page.

Live production screen — package step, with progress indicator (step 4 of 6)
Live production screen — purchase step: manual add-ons with cashback, coupon code, running total
Live production screen — multi-item cart: each package (exam bundle, admission course, precourse) can be settled in full or held independently, with a running order total

Why a numbered wizard, not a long form

Enrollment bundles a lot of decisions — objective, modality, course, package, group, add-ons. Splitting it into a visible, numbered sequence (with completed steps checked off in a running summary) keeps a first-time visitor oriented instead of facing one long, intimidating form.

Add-ons and incentives live inside the flow, not after it

Study manuals with cashback and a coupon-code field sit directly in the purchase step, next to a running subtotal/total — upsell and discount logic the visitor can react to immediately, instead of discovering it at a separate checkout screen.

Case Study 03

Admin Dashboard — untangling how prospects, calls, and course authoring actually work

Operations staff were manually cross-checking prospect and call data across course, event, and general-inquiry categories — the system didn't reflect how they actually needed to triage and assign work. I redesigned the information architecture and the authoring flows non-technical academic staff use every day.

Live production screen — WhatsApp prospect thread inside the call-assignment module
Live production screen — student record with a side action panel (credential, documents, groups, exams)
Live production screen — payment status, unifying web, in-branch, and kiosk payment options
Live production screen — study-manual shipping tracker with a 3-step progress indicator

What I redesigned

  • Prospect-to-call segmentation (course / event / general inquiry) with priority and assignee logic, replacing manual cross-checks between systems.
  • The authoring flows academic staff use to create and configure exam simulations, courses, and packages.
  • The roles-and-permissions model underneath, defining who can see and edit what across the platform.

Why it mattered

A data-integrity issue in the catalog or endpoint layer isn't just a bug — if operations can't trust the data driving their queue, they route back to manual work. I treated those diagnoses as trust problems first, then fixed the source. I also added automated (Playwright) end-to-end tests over the communications workflows so the redesigned experience wouldn't regress silently.

Case Study 04 — Product Ownership

Research Resource Tracking System (ESCOM, IPN)

Here I wasn't just the designer — I was the Product Owner and the primary point of contact for ESCOM's research stakeholders, which meant owning the UI/UX decisions and defending them.

Scope

Designed and delivered 13 screens/components on top of a Django (MVT) / PostgreSQL backend for end-to-end tracking of research resources.

Role

Ran requirements sessions, demos, and acceptance directly with research stakeholders, and acted as the design decision-maker bridging the development team, other designers, and the client.
